R1037.rationale:
The collapse of the 2018 revitalized peace agreement and the disbandment of the unity government have dramatically increased the risk of South Sudan sliding back into full-scale civil conflict. The March 2025 arrest of First Vice President Riek Machar of the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-in-Opposition by President Salva Kiir has reignited ethnically charged fighting between Dinka and Nuer armed forces, with clashes already concentrated in Jonglei and Upper Nile states. Up to 300,000 newly displaced people add to the approximately two million already internally displaced and over ten million – two-thirds of the population – requiring some form of humanitarian assistance, including 7.5 million projected to face food insecurity during the April–July lean season. South Sudan has suffered from chronic violence since independence. The collapse of the peace framework ahead of elections, accompanied by the re-emergence of organised, ethnically mobilised armed groups, represents the risk of a return to full-scale civil war.
Several factors increase the likelihood of deterioration into civil war. The taking and retaking of Akobo signals an escalation beyond the fragmented, subnational violence that characterised the 2018–2024 period, with organised armed groups now contesting territory at a scale not seen since the first civil war. The mobilisation of Nuer armed groups, including the White Army, suggests this is a coordinated insurgency with the capacity to sustain prolonged fighting. Uganda's continued deployment of troops in support of Kiir's Government risks drawing the conflict into a broader regional confrontation, and spillover from Sudan and Ethiopia could further destabilise border areas. Over 1.36 million people have already arrived in South Sudan from Sudan since April 2023, with services in border areas stretched to breaking point; an additional 380,000 arrivals are projected by the end of 2026. The planned December 2026 elections, already twice postponed, will intensify political competition and may become a flashpoint for renewed violence, whether they proceed or are cancelled again. ([ICG 25/03/2026](https://www.crisisgroup.org/cmt/africa/south-sudan/halting-south-sudans-slide-war), [ISS 30/03/2026](https://issafrica.org/iss-today/race-against-time-to-stabilise-south-sudan-as-elections-loom), [OCHA 12/02/2026](https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/south-sudan/south-sudan-humanitarian-needs-and-response-plan-2026-january-2026), [OCHA 16/04/2026](https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/south-sudan/south-sudan-humanitarian-update-1-17-april-2026), [MSF 30/01/2026](https://www.msf.org/south-sudan-government-blocks-opposition-held-areas-humanitarian-access))

triggers.title: Economic collapse drives predatory violence by armed actors on both sides
triggers.description: Prolonged economic decline has left both sides severely weakened. Depleted state coffers and irregular pay have driven desertions and eroded morale, leaving government forces overstretched and increasingly reliant on proxy militias. With formal resourcing exhausted, offensives by government forces and militias have become as much about extracting taxes and looting civilian populations as achieving military objectives. Opposition forces face comparable pressures, with communal militias motivated more by the prospect of loot than political strategy. As both sides are compelled to prey on the communities they operate in, this dynamic risks transforming localised clashes into a self-sustaining cycle of violence, in which continued conflict becomes an economic necessity for armed actors, reducing incentives to negotiate and compounding an already acute humanitarian crisis. R1059.rationale:
After the elections in June 2026, Abelardo de la Espriella’s win as Colombia's new President signalled a major change in the country's stance towards non-state armed groups (NSAGs) and drug trafficking organisations. The President-elect has since announced an end to peace negotiations and a nationwide military offensive to begin once he takes office on 7 August, including a 90-day security crackdown involving military deployments, aerial operations, and coca eradication measures.
This shift may increase the risk of clashes, civilian casualties, displacement, and confinement, particularly in Pacific Coast departments, including Cauca, Chocó, Nariño, and Valle del Cauca, as well as in Norte de Santander and Putumayo, which were among Colombia’s most conflict-affected areas in 2025.
This risk is compounded by the significant strengthening of NSAGs in recent years. Armed group membership has grown substantially since 2022. Armed groups have simultaneously expanded into new territories, adopted new warfare tactics, including the use of explosive drones, and extended social control against communities, including curfews and checkpoints. Ahead of the anticipated offensive, NSAGs are expected to intensify operations to consolidate territorial control, while retaliatory actions during the crackdown could further increase civilian harm. In response, the elected President has proposed Plan Colombia 2.0, aimed at recovering NSAG-controlled territory, eradicating coca cultivation and illegal mining (the primary financing sources for armed groups), and securing record investment in state armed forces, with the political and financial support of the US Government.
As a result, July, the month preceding the new Government's inauguration, is expected to see an intensification of NSAG violence as armed groups seek to consolidate territorial control and prepare ahead of the anticipated military offensive. Over the first 90-day period (August–October), a marked increase in armed clashes with state forces is expected, a trend that should persist throughout the remainder of 2026. These dynamics will directly affect civilian populations in the departments highlighted, where most rural and Indigenous communities reside.
Planned government reforms, including major cuts to state bureaucracy and measures targeting officials linked to the previous administration, could also increase political tensions and trigger social mobilisation, adding a civil unrest dimension to the risk.
A historic ‘Super El Niño’ event, forecast to intensify through late 2026, is expected to compound these dynamics. Authorities are warning of extreme heat, drought, and water shortages, with national implications for food security. This adds further pressure on communities in the departments covered by this risk, where access to food is already constrained by confinement and mobility restrictions linked to armed group activity. 
([El País 21/06/2026](https://elpais.com/america-colombia/elecciones-presidenciales/2026-06-21/las-propuestas-de-abelardo-de-la-espriella-seguridad-de-mano-dura-reduccion-del-estado-y-libertades-tributarias.html), [FIP 30/01/2026](https://ideaspaz.org/publicaciones/investigaciones-analisis/2026-01/27-000-combatientes-y-record-en-disputas-el-deterioro-de-la-seguridad-marca-el-inicio-de-2026), [Valora Analitik 17/12/2025](https://www.valoraanalitik.com/grupos-armados-en-colombia-aumentaron-casi-70-desde-2022-crecen-homicidios-y-secuestros/), [Defensores de la Patria accessed 06/07/2026](https://defensoresdelapatria.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/PROPUESTAS-DEL-TIGRE.pdf), [AJ 22/06/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/6/22/far-right-de-la-espriella-elected-colombia-president-whats-next), [NPR 21/06/2026](https://www.npr.org/2026/06/21/nx-s1-5865676/delaespriella-colombia-election), [Atlantic Council 22/06/2026](https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/dispatches/experts-react-what-a-president-abelardo-de-la-espriella-means-for-colombia-and-beyond/), [The City Paper 21/05/2026](https://thecitypaperbogota.com/news/colombia-on-guard-as-super-el-nino-threatens-record-heat-drought-and-food-security/))

R1043.rationale:
Since early 2026, the conflict in Sudan has evolved from a humanitarian crisis affecting Chad into a direct security threat to eastern border areas. Repeated drone strikes, cross-border incursions, and clashes involving fighters aligned with the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) have already caused casualties on Chadian territory, including around Tine and other border regions. These incidents indicate a growing risk that the Sudan conflict could generate sustained military confrontations, proxy violence, or retaliatory attacks inside Chad. This risk is increasingly characterised by the possibility of sustained military confrontation on Chadian territory involving RSF, SAF-aligned groups, and associated proxy forces operating along the Chad–Sudan border.

This risk is driven by a convergence of security, economic, and political factors. The Chad–Sudan border has become a strategic corridor for the movement of fuel, arms, gold, and military supplies supporting groups involved in the Sudan conflict. Competition over these routes has transformed border areas into contested spaces where violence increasingly follows smuggling and supply networks. Recent attacks suggest a shift from incidental spillover to deliberate projection of force into Chadian territory.

The conflict is also aggravating existing vulnerabilities in Chad. Fractures within cross-border Zaghawa community networks, which remain influential within Chad’s security apparatus, have deepened as communities react to violence in Darfur and perceptions of Chad’s involvement in the conflict. Continued violence in Darfur, combined with Chad’s historical role in Sudanese proxy conflicts, increases the risk of elite defections, armed realignments, and renewed cross-border mobilisation. Historical patterns of proxy warfare between Chad and Sudan may also re-emerge, including support to armed groups and militias operating across the border, increasing the likelihood of retaliatory attacks and further regional destabilisation.

Over the next one to three months, further RSF incursions, SAF-backed proxy activity, or competition over border corridors could increase cross-border violence, displacement, protection risks, and humanitarian needs in eastern Chad. Additional attacks or retaliations would likely worsen conditions in provinces already hosting large numbers of refugees and returnees, further straining regional services, humanitarian operations, and community relations. The risk is not limited to humanitarian spillover and increasingly involves the possibility of sustained confrontation on Chadian territory involving RSF, SAF-aligned groups, and associated proxy forces. ([Africa Center for Strategic Studies 09/03/2026](https://africacenter.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Chad-Risks-Instability.pdf), [ACLED 08/04/2026](https://acleddata.com/update/africa-overview-april-2026), [Global Initiative 06/03/2026](https://globalinitiative.net/analysis/how-border-criminal-economies-are-drawing-chad-further-into-sudans-conflict/), [ISS Africa 03/04/2025](https://issafrica.org/iss-today/urgent-au-action-could-defuse-rising-chad-sudan-tensions), [RFI 13/05/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/fr/afrique/20260513-tchad-de-nouvelles-frappes-enregistr%C3%A9es-%C3%A0-la-fronti%C3%A8re-soudanaise-font-craindre-le-pire), [UNHCR 18/05/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/chad/core-emergency-situation-chad-update-arrivals-sudan-17-may-2026), [UNFPA 15/05/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/chad/unfpa-situation-report-chad-humanitarian-response-1-30-april-2026))

R1069.rationale:
By 28 August 2026, an estimated 700–1,000 military personnel were conducting clearance operations around the long-stalled Dawei Special Economic Zone (SEZ) in Yebyu township after a late-June order to protect the strategic projects. Since 9 July, fighting, raids, arson, looting, arbitrary arrests, and killings have displaced more than 4,500 people from eight Nabule villages. Renewed fighting near the SEZ from 21–22 August caused further civilian displacement. More than 2,000 people were displaced from ten villages in Thayetchaung township in August.
The concentration of military deployments around the project area, following orders to protect strategic infrastructure and agreements to revive the project, indicates that the operation is intended to secure the SEZ. The SEZ is a long-stalled port and industrial zone planned to include a deep-sea port, coal-fired power plant, oil refinery, and liquefied natural gas facilities. The risk is more immediate because Myanmar and Russia revived the project in 2025, signed a June 2026 power plant agreement, and included the Dawei port, refinery, and power plant in their August Moscow agreements. The timing of these deals and the deployment, alongside clashes with the Karen National Liberation Army (KNLA) near Wet Chaung, makes control of the project area a current strategic objective rather than a remote development scenario.
Over the next six months, military efforts to secure the SEZ are likely to include attempts to control Highway 8, the main north–south route through Tanintharyi, and the Dawei–Htee Khee road, which connects the project area through Myitta to the Thailand border. These routes are important for moving troops and supplies and would support future port and SEZ operations. R1062.rationale:
Humanitarian needs, particularly related to protection, food security, and access, are increasing and are at high risk of deteriorating further along the Durand Line between Afghanistan and Pakistan given the conflict escalation and air strikes between the two countries. Hostilities have spiked since 28 June 2026 along Aghanistan’s border provinces, including Kunar, Paktia, and Paktika, when a Pakistani attack killed 28 civilians and wounded 49. Pakistani authorities stated that the strikes targeted the Tehrik-e Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which they held responsible for a deadly militant attack in Karachi that killed three security personnel. Pakistan has consistently accused Afghanistan of harbouring armed groups responsible for attacks on Pakistani security forces and civilians, including the TTP, which Islamabad accuses of operating from Afghan soil. Afghanistan has denied these allegations and threatened retaliation against Pakistan for the air strikes.
The latest attack comes as part of a series of tit-for-tat attacks between Afghanistan and Pakistan that started in February. After launching Operation Ghazab lil Haq on 21 February, Pakistani authorities declared open war against Afghanistan's Interim Taliban Authority. Despite a two-week ceasefire beginning on 8 April negotiated by China, these attacks have continued, forming a pattern of ‘coercive diplomacy’ between the two countries. This coercive diplomacy has seen fighting continue until it becomes less productive for either side, at which point they briefly return to negotiations until a new security incident restarts the cycle. This pattern is expected to persist in waves over the next three to six months rather than resolve into a stable ceasefire.
The current tension heightens protection risks for civilians in border-adjacent Afghan provinces (Khost, Kunar, Nangarhar, Nuristan, Paktia, and Paktika), including casualties and injuries from cross-border air strikes and ground attacks, as well as exposure to explosive remnants of war and unexploded ordnance in areas affected by shelling.
Displacement towards other regions of Afghanistan is expected to persist over the next three to six months. The closure of and restricted movement at the Torkham, Chaman, and other crossings along the Durand Line, whether from active conflict or checkpoint closures, could trap civilians in insecure areas or block access to services on the other side. Host communities already sheltering IDPs and returnees face added strain, raising the risk of tension and disputes over limited resources and services.
The closure of border crossings has also halted transit flows and delayed humanitarian and commercial supplies. Afghanistan is highly dependent on food imports, as domestic production cannot meet national demand. This dependence, combined with the depletion of harvest stocks in September and declining agricultural labour opportunities from the seasonal downturn in October, is likely to worsen food insecurity. As a result, market dependence is expected to increase, reducing household income and heightening the risk of food consumption gaps. ([CFR 18/03/2026](https://www.cfr.org/articles/why-are-the-afghan-taliban-and-pakistan-in-an-open-war), [The Guardian 29/06/2026](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/jun/29/pakistan-deadly-airstrikes-afghanistan-border), [HRW 15/07/2026](https://www.hrw.org/news/2026/07/15/pakistani-strikes-in-afghanistan-raise-civilian-casualty-concerns), [UNAMA 11/05/2026](https://unama.unmissions.org/sites/default/files/2026-05/English%20-%20UNAMA%20HRS%20paper%20on%20cross-border%20civilian%20casualties%20-%20Jan-Mar%202026_Updated_11.05.26.pdf), [WFP 26/06/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/afghanistan/food-security-under-pressure-impacts-middle-east-crisis-and-pakistan-conflict-afghanistan-june-2026), [OCHA 28/04/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/afghanistan/afghanistan-situation-update-4-humanitarian-impact-afghanistan-pakistan-military-escalation-28-april-2026), [NPR 03/04/2026](https://www.npr.org/2026/04/03/g-s1-116299/pakistan-says-a-new-round-of-peace-talks-with-afghanistan-is-underway-in-china), [Reuters 02/04/2026](https://www.aol.com/articles/pakistan-says-talks-afghanistan-end-071917568.html), [UNAMA 29/06/2026](https://unama.unmissions.org/en/news/unama-statement-on-civilian-casualties))

R1066.rationale:
Violence involving Boko Haram and Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) is rising after five years of declining lethality in the Lake Chad Basin. More than 300 clashes involving the two groups were recorded in the first quarter of 2026, 30% above the previous quarter, while militant Islamist-linked fatalities increased by 28% over the past year, reaching their highest level since 2015. Nigeria accounted for 87% of these fatalities, with Borno remaining the expected epicentre, followed by affected areas of Adamawa and Yobe.
The escalation is expected to be driven by two related developments. While regional forces have concentrated military operations against ISWAP, Boko Haram has regrouped and rebuilt its capacity to launch coordinated attacks against military bases. At the same time, the May killing of senior ISWAP leader Abu-Bilal Al Minuki is expected to trigger retaliatory attacks and greater competition between factions for territorial influence and legitimacy. ISWAP has overrun at least 16 Nigerian military bases over the past year, while its increasing use of improvised explosive devices and reconnaissance drones enhances its capacity to identify, isolate, and attack military positions, increasing the operational threat posed by the group.
Over the next three to six months, there is a very high probability that intensified insurgent attacks and military counteroperations will increase civilian casualties, displacement, and humanitarian access constraints across the basin. Violence is expected to remain concentrated in Borno, with continued spillover into Adamawa and Yobe, where Boko Haram and ISWAP are likely to intensify attacks on civilians, military positions, and transport routes. Escalating violence in northeastern Nigeria is expected to generate additional refugee movements into Niger's Diffa region, while military pressure and cross-border armed group movements may contribute to increased attacks, abductions, and disruptions to fishing and trade in Cameroon’s Far North, as well as renewed displacement and protection risks in Chad’s Lac province. These cross-border displacement dynamics and parallel insecurity are expected to reverse recent stabilisation gains and generate additional humanitarian needs across the Lake Chad Basin. Persistent tension in Badakhshan, driven by disputes over mining resources, ethnic differences, contested territorial control, and grievances over Interim Taliban Authority (ITA) governance, risk creating recurrent instability and protection risks for communities.
Armed opposition to the ITA has been building in the province over the course of 2026. ACLED recorded 22 anti-ITA armed-opposition events in Badakhshan between January–July 2026, up from just four between June–December 2025. While the recent surrender of Fateh-aligned fighters has eased the immediate risk of renewed clashes, the ITA's broader efforts to consolidate control over powerful opposition commanders and curb their influence are likely to generate resentment among these groups, increasing the risk of further infighting.
ACLED forecasts at least 34 violent events nationwide in September 2026, of which 19 (roughly 56%) are projected to occur in Badakhshan alone, meaning a 17% rise in violence against civilians compared to the previous month's average. This indicates Badakhshan province is becoming a potential point for national conflict risk.
The province has valuable mineral deposits, including gold and lapis lazuli, and has long been contested. Recent clashes were triggered by the ITA suspension of gold mining activities in parts of the province to disarm fighters of opposition groups.
Clashes have occurred across multiple districts in 2026, including a brief seizure of the Yaftal-e Sufla district headquarters and Afghanistan Freedom Front clashes with ITA forces in Zebak in July. Repeated fighting over district centres risks triggering intermittent displacement as families flee active front lines and may expose residents to crossfire, checkpoint violence, and casualties. Badakhshan’s current context indicates a risk of rising displacement and protection needs, reduced humanitarian access to respond to them, and a deteriorating food security outlook. R1072.rationale:
Islamic State Mozambique (ISM) activity in northern Mozambique has increasingly shifted towards mobile, small-group operations as a response to intensified military pressure from Mozambican security forces and their regional partners. Increased patrols, aerial surveillance, and continued counterinsurgency operations have reduced non-state armed groups' capacity to hold territory. As a result, ISM have increasingly dispersed from areas under intensified military pressure in Macomia district towards southern and western Cabo Delgado province. ISM have moved through Quissanga, Mecufi, and Meluco towards Ancuabe and Chiure districts, while other groups moved west towards Montepuez district and subsequently towards Niassa province. One group also crossed into Erati district in Nampula province.
Over the next six months, continued military pressure in Cabo Delgado is expected to further disperse ISM fighters towards areas with weaker security coverage. Remote forested areas and limited state presence in parts of Marrupa, Mecula, and Mavago districts, which have had some pockets of attacks, provide opportunities for small groups to move and conduct more attacks. ISM have increasingly targeted informal gold mining sites for looting and ransom, while attacks on vehicles and road users have generated additional income through extortion. In Niassa, the July–November hunting season also increases the presence of hunting camps, tourism operators, and vehicles in remote areas, creating potential high-value targets for ransom and material gains. If ISM establish a presence in Montepuez, Marrupa, Mecula, and Mavago districts, these activities could provide alternative sources of revenue and sustain their operations. ([ACLED 05/08/2026](https://acleddata.com/update/mozambique-conflict-monitor-update-august-2026), [IOM 24/06/2026](https://dtm.iom.int/reports/mozambique-movement-alert-report-163-24-june-2026), [ACLED 08/09/2026](https://acleddata.com/update/mozambique-conflict-monitor-update-september-2026), [OCHA 08/09/2026](https://www.unocha.org/publications/report/mozambique/mozambique-2026-humanitarian-response-conflict-overview-july-2026-enpt), [Gov.UK accessed 22/09/2026](https://www.gov.uk/foreign-travel-advice/mozambique/regional-risks))

R1061.rationale:
There is a high probability that Israeli forces will formally declare and physically enclose a permanent military exclusion zone east of the Yellow Line in the period leading up to Israel's October 2026 parliamentary elections, progressively reducing the territory accessible to civilians and humanitarian responders.
Since the 10 October 2025 ceasefire, Israeli forces have steadily expanded their military footprint beyond the initial demarcation line through tank advances, repeated evacuation orders, the construction of defensive positions, and localised operations. The Israeli-controlled area had expanded from 53% of Gaza Strip at the ceasefire to 64.9% by June 2026, with the trend notably intensifying late into the month. The Armed Conflict Location & Event Data reports that events reflecting Yellow Line expansion and associated military movements increased from an average of fewer than four events per month between October 2025 and mid-June 2026 to 22 events between 18 June and 17 July 2026, a more than fivefold increase.

During the same period, activity by the Shuja’iyya Popular Defense Forces led by Rami Hilles, an anti-Hamas Palestinian armed group operating with Israeli support, also increased. Between 30 June and 9 July, the group carried out three recorded incidents targeting IDP camps in Gaza city's At Tuffah and Shuja’iyya neighbourhoods, including reported abductions and raids, indicating increasingly complex security dynamics around the expanding Yellow Line.

The period preceding Israel's October 2026 elections has a high probability of reinforcing this trajectory rather than prompting a fundamental shift in military strategy. With far-right coalition partners Otzma Yehudit and Religious Zionism continuing to advocate expanding Israeli control over Gaza and negotiations on a durable ceasefire and post-conflict governance remaining stalled, the Likud-led caretaker government, in place since the Knesset dissolved on 17 July 2026, will very probably prioritise maintaining operational momentum in Gaza while avoiding the political and military risks associated with a large-scale offensive.

Territorial expansion is expected to continue through a combination of military and engineering measures that progressively transform temporary military positions into more permanent areas of control. Israeli forces are likely to continue advancing the Yellow Line through localised incursions supported by repeated evacuation orders, the demolition of buildings and agricultural land, and the construction of additional military infrastructure, including outposts, surveillance positions, access roads, trenches, and earthen barriers. Recent satellite imagery indicates that Israel has already constructed more than 23km of earth berms and trenches along parts of the Yellow Line, creating a fortified corridor that extends across central Gaza and, in some locations, beyond the original ceasefire demarcation. These measures are likely to be accompanied by the continued expansion of military exclusion zones and restrictions on civilian movement, allowing Israeli forces to consolidate control without undertaking a single large-scale offensive. ([BIPP 06/03/2026](https://www.bakerinstitute.org/research/israeli-elections-cast-doubt-gaza-peace-plan), [NPR 23/07/2026](https://www.npr.org/2026/07/23/nx-s1-5891506/israel-will-hold-elections-this-fall-gadi-eisenkott-could-be-the-next-prime-minister), [Chatham House 22/07/2026](https://www.chathamhouse.org/2026/07/israels-general-election-will-be-no-other), [CNN 20/07/2026](https://edition.cnn.com/2026/07/20/middleeast/israel-far-right-settlements-gaza-intl), [The Conversation 24/07/2026](https://theconversation.com/as-israel-prepares-for-october-election-the-government-is-accelerating-its-land-grab-in-the-west-bank-and-gaza-288286), [DAWN 21/07/2026](https://dawnmena.org/israels-elections-will-not-end-its-genocidal-and-expansionist-policies/), [ACLED accessed 25/07/2026](https://acleddata.com/conflict-data/data-export-tool), [Haaretz 07/07/2026](https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/israel-security/2026-07-07/ty-article/.premium/as-netanyahu-battles-for-votes-he-could-reignite-gaza-fighting/0000019f-390c-d62f-a39f-7d2c08a00000), [LWJ 19/10/2025](https://www.longwarjournal.org/archives/2025/10/profiles-of-anti-hamas-militias-in-the-gaza-strip.php), [AP accessed 01/08/2026](https://apnews.com/article/israel-gaza-yellow-line-barrier-ceasefire-941ed80f6d4398ce88916f6b08753dd8), [TOI 17/07/2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/knesset-votes-on-official-dispersal-of-parliament-wrapping-up-final-legislative-blitz/), [AJ 22/07/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/7/22/creeping-death-israel-weaponises-yellow-line-to-annex-gaza))

R1073.rationale:
The E1 settlement plan is a longstanding Israeli initiative that was revived in July 2025 after four years of suspension and approved for advancement by the Israeli Government on 20 August 2025. The plan aims to expand Ma’ale Adumim municipality and create a continuous built-up area between the Israeli settlements and Jerusalem city. Its implementation could further fragment the West Bank, particularly by disrupting geographic contiguity between central and southern areas, and increase the likelihood of severing East Jerusalem from the rest of the occupied West Bank. Its advancement could accelerate the displacement of entire Bedouin communities in the area, generating additional humanitarian needs.
Implementation has accelerated in 2026. In August, Israel issued a tender for 1,234 housing units in E1, followed on 17 September by a further 2,167 units, bringing the total to 3,401. Bidding on the 2,167-unit tender was scheduled to open on 25 October, two days before Israel's 27 October parliamentary elections.
Government efforts to advance the tenders before the election could accelerate implementation of the approved plan and trigger a faster-paced displacement. The awarding of tenders would allow the Israeli Government to move faster towards infrastructure works and construction, making the project more difficult for a future government to reverse. Implementation could accelerate if the tender process proceeds despite the postponement and the current Government retains power after the election. Court challenges or an election outcome that produces a government less supportive of E1 could, however, delay further implementation.([OCHA 21/08/2025](https://www.ochaopt.org/content/humanitarian-situation-update-316-west-bank), [OCHA 16/07/2025](https://www.ochaopt.org/content/humanitarian-situation-update-305-west-bank), [MAP 19/08/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/occupied-palestinian-territory/map-warns-palestinian-healthcare-workers-face-mounting-attacks-amid-escalating-west-bank-violence), [BBC 20/08/2026](https://www.bbc.com/arabic/articles/cvgx03d488yo), [OCHA 28/09/2026](https://www.ochaopt.org/content/humanitarian-situation-report-25-september-2026), [OCHA 25/05/2026](https://www.ochaopt.org/content/humanitarian-situation-report-25-may-2026), [Reuters 17/09/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/israel-adds-tender-2167-housing-units-settlement-expansion-plan-rights-groups-2026-09-17/), [HRW 19/08/2026](https://www.hrw.org/news/2026/08/19/west-bank-illegal-e1-settlement-tender-opens-for-bids), [Al Arabiya 24/08/2026](https://www.alarabiya.net/arab-and-world/2026/08/24/%D9%85%D8%B3%D8%A4%D9%88%D9%84-%D8%A7%D8%B3%D8%B1%D8%A7%D8%A6%D9%8A%D9%84%D9%8A-%D9%8A%D8%AD%D8%B0%D8%B1-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%B6%D9%81%D8%A9-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%BA%D8%B1%D8%A8%D9%8A%D8%A9-%D8%A7%D9%85%D8%A7%D9%85-%D8%AE%D8%B7%D8%B1-%D8%A7%D9%86%D9%81%D8%AC%D8%A7%D8%B1), [WAFA 17/09/2026](https://english.wafa.ps/Pages/Details/174831), [Peace Now 19/08/2026](https://peacenow.org.il/en/e1-tender-published-and-open-for-bidding), [Times of Israel 27/09/2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/ag-postpones-tenders-for-e1-settlement-project-smotrich-accuses-her-of-election-meddling/), [The New Arab 27/09/2026](https://www.newarab.com/news/israel-attorney-general-delays-e1-settlement-tender))

R1065.rationale:
On 13 July 2026, the Iran-backed de-facto authority (DFA) in the north of Yemen (also known as the Houthis) announced the end of a de facto period of de-escalation with Saudi Arabia and the Saudi-backed Internationally Recognized Government (IRG) of Yemen, increasing the risk of renewed cross-border and intra-Yemeni hostilities following a series of retaliatory actions. On the same day, the IRG said it had struck Sana'a International Airport to prevent an Iranian aircraft from landing, while the DFA accused Saudi Arabia of carrying out the attack. The DFA subsequently retaliated by launching missile and drone attacks against Abha International Airport, marking the first attack on Saudi territory since the 2022 truce. On 20 July, the DFA announced a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia, describing it as a response to Saudi restrictions on DFA-controlled airports and seaports. The DFA has already targeted several vessels, including two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, in an attempt to enforce the blockade.
Fighting has also intensified between the DFA and the IRG along front lines in Al Hodeidah, Al Jawf, Ma’rib, and Ta’iz, predating but compounded by the deterioration in Saudi–Houthi relations. Saudi Arabia is the main IRG backer, and the deterioration in Saudi–Houthi relations has already prompted expanded military involvement. From 24–25 July, the Saudi-led coalition conducted strikes in Al Hodeidah, while the IRG air force struck DFA missile and drone launch sites and weapons facilities in Ma'rib and Al Jawf. These developments indicate that the escalation has expanded beyond isolated cross-border retaliation, increasing the risk of sustained intra-Yemeni conflict.
The first cross-border attack on Saudi Arabia since the truce is significant because it signals that both parties are becoming increasingly willing to use direct military force to pursue their objectives, weakening one of the key restraints that has sustained the de facto ceasefire. Both Saudi Arabia and the DFA have incentives to avoid a renewed large-scale conflict. Saudi Arabia seeks to protect its economic interests and avoid another costly war, while the DFA is unlikely to escalate unless it perceives increased Saudi military involvement or an opportunity to improve its strategic position. A miscalculation could trigger the renewal of conflict. Further attacks on Saudi territory or attempts to enforce a blockade of the Bab Al Mandab Strait would increase the likelihood of expanded or sustained Saudi and international military involvement in the Red Sea and Yemen. Saudi Arabia has already announced plans for a multinational maritime defence coalition on 30 July 2026.
Escalations between the DFA and Saudi Arabia would likely intensify fighting between the DFA and the Saudi-backed IRG, further restricting humanitarian access. Saudi air strikes on seaports and airports would disrupt commercial and humanitarian imports, triggering new displacement. Supply chain disruptions would increase commodity prices and erode purchasing power. Any disruption to shipping through the Bab Al Mandab Strait would also have cascading impacts on regional and global supply chains while aggravating needs in a country where over 22 million people require humanitarian assistance and 18.3 million are acutely food-insecure. ([OCHA 29/03/2026](https://yemen.un.org/en/312711-ocha-yemen-yemen-humanitarian-needs-and-response-plan-2026-march-2026), [JP 25/07/2026](https://www.jpost.com/middle-east/article-903606), [Reuters 24/07/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/yemen-teeters-towards-renewed-war-shadow-iran-conflict-2026-07-24/), [ICG 17/07/2026](https://www.crisisgroup.org/qna/middle-east-north-africa/yemen-iran-saudi-arabia/yemens-de-facto-truce-risk-how-prevent-return-war), [AJ 05/07/2026](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/7/5/at-least-15-yemeni-government-troops-killed-in-hodeidah-fighting), [The Guardian 23/07/2026](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/jul/23/houthis-claim-attack-ship-tanker-saudi-arabia-red-sea), [Reuters 23/07/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/houthis-say-they-attacked-saudi-tankers-red-sea-threatening-new-chokepoint-iran-2026-07-23/), [Arab News 25/07/2026](https://www.arabnews.com/node/2652234/middle-east), [SPA 25/07/2026](https://www.spa.gov.sa/en/N2640956))

R1054.rationale: Since 2025, RSF has expanded its long-range drone capabilities, including kamikaze munitions able to target infrastructure far inside SAF-controlled areas. Northern and River Nile states have already experienced repeated drone attacks on infrastructure, including strikes affecting Merowe Dam and associated power facilities. These attacks have mostly caused temporary disruptions rather than sustained structural damage, but they demonstrate intent and reach. The risk would increase if SAF-RSF fighting intensifies and RSF continues receiving external support that improves its long-range strike capacity. RSF has a clear strategic incentive to target Merowe Dam because it is Sudan's largest hydroelectric dam and supports electricity generation, irrigation, and economic activity across areas under SAF control. Disrupting the dam or the associated electricity grid would allow RSF to increase pressure on SAF governance, undermine public confidence, and disrupt services in areas away from front lines. While imminent large-scale escalation in Northern state is not clearly indicated, the dam's strategic importance makes damaging attacks a credible medium-term risk. R1055.rationale: Deteriorating humanitarian conditions, aid shortfalls, and insecurity in eastern Chad are increasingly pushing Sudanese refugees to return to unsafe areas in Darfur, particularly West Darfur. Return movements rose in early 2026, with April arrivals into West Darfur nearly doubling compared with November 2025 levels. Many returnees cited access to resources, services, and humanitarian assistance as a main driver, suggesting that deteriorating conditions in displacement are influencing return decisions. Funding cuts and reduced assistance in Chad have weakened refugee coping capacity and strained already overstretched refugee-hosting areas. Planned relocations away from the Sudan border, following RSF cross-border attacks and Chadian military deployment, may increase uncertainty and pressure on some households to return prematurely. Political instability and tensions within Chad, including dynamics linked to alleged external support for RSF and tensions among groups affected by violence in Darfur, could make refugee-hosting areas less predictable. These factors may increase unsafe returns to Darfur despite continuing insecurity, limited services, and protection risks. ([IOM 13/04/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/sudan/dtm-sudan-displacement-and-return-snapshot-update-4-12-april-2026), [RFI 24/03/2026](https://www.rfi.fr/en/africa/20260324-chad-relocates-refugees-amid-rising-tensions-at-border-with-sudan), [IOM 26/01/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/sudan/dtm-sudan-displacement-and-return-snapshot-update-1-26-january-2026), [UN 17/02/2026](https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/02/1166979), [UNHCR accessed 27/05/2026](https://data.unhcr.org/en/country/tcd), [Reuters 23/03/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/africa/chad-relocates-sudan-refugees-army-deploys-near-border-2026-03-23/), [ICG 01/09/2025](https://www.crisisgroup.org/cmt/africa/chad-sudan/preserver-la-stabilite-du-tchad-face-au-conflit-soudanais))

R1051.rationale: The continuation or expansion of trade bans imposed in late 2025 by Khartoum, Northern, and North Kordofan states on the movement of goods into RSF-controlled areas would likely further restrict supplies to West Kordofan. These restrictions would affect food, fuel, medicines, agricultural inputs, and other essential commodities. West Kordofan is particularly exposed because it is landlocked and has historically depended on supply chains from northern and eastern Sudan, including routes through Khartoum, Red Sea ports, and Egypt. As formal routes become more restricted, markets are likely to rely increasingly on informal supply routes that are longer, more insecure, and more expensive because of checkpoints, unofficial taxation, transport delays, and insecurity. Alternative routes through Al Na'am market near Abyei provide some supply capacity but are limited and vulnerable to shocks, including fires, border tensions, and armed-party interference. If bans persist, supply shortages and price increases are likely to deepen food insecurity and market fragmentation across the state.  ([Darfur24 23/12/2025](https://www.darfur24.com/2025/12/23/%D8%BA%D9%84%D8%A7%D8%A1-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%B9%D9%8A%D8%B4%D8%A9-%D9%8A%D9%87%D8%AF%D8%AF-%D9%83%D8%B1%D8%AF%D9%81%D8%A7%D9%86-%D8%A8%D8%B9%D8%AF-%D8%AD%D8%B8%D8%B1-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%AE%D8%B1%D8%B7/), [ST 20/12/2025](https://sudantribune.com/article/308450), [SMF 31/12/2025](https://sudanmediaforum.org/en/blocking-the-passage-of-goods-and-merchandise-to-western-sudan-another-war-waged-by-khartoum-against-the-people/), [FEWS NET 11/03/2026](https://fews.net/east-africa/sudan/food-security-outlook/february-2026), [REACH 05/03/2026](https://reliefweb.int/report/sudan/sudan-trend-analysis-january-2026-comparative-price-trends-darfur-and-greater-kordofan-july-december-2025))

R1068.rationale:
Since the fall of Bashar Al Assad in December 2024, Israel’s military presence in southern Syria has evolved from incursions into sustained territorial control. By early 2026, Israeli forces have expanded beyond the UN-monitored 1974 separation line into parts of Quneitra and western Dar’a, establishing military posts, outposts, and checkpoints. By mid-2026, the presence had become increasingly entrenched, with regular patrols and ground activity beyond the former separation area. Further expansion of positions, checkpoints, or closed military zones would indicate movement towards a more permanent security zone. Sustained territorial control or restrictions on civilian access could increase local resistance and create conditions for further expansion towards areas linked to As Sweida.
Two pathways could accelerate or formalise this existing trajectory in the next three to six months. One is the revival of a proposal for a humanitarian corridor, first suggested in 2025 by Israeli officials to provide aid for Druze in As Sweida, particularly if renewed violence in As Sweida gives Israel a justification to intervene on behalf of the Druze and expand in southern Syria. The proposed corridor would connect the governorate with the Golan area, including Hader near Mount Hermon and Druze villages along the Syrian Golan. Although the proposal was previously rejected by the Syrian transitional Government, renewed violence or deterioration in As Sweida could bring it back into discussions and provide a pretext for expanding Israeli control or establishing protected access through southern Syria. While Israel framed its military intervention during the July 2025 violence as protecting the Druze, Druze opinion remains divided. One senior spiritual leader, Sheikh Hikmat Al Hijri, has welcomed Israeli involvement, while the other two have consistently rejected foreign interference, and As Sweida's Druze security chief warned it had complicated reconciliation.
A second pathway is the activity of Israeli settlers seeking to establish a permanent presence. The Pioneers of Bashan,  an Israeli settler movement, have repeatedly attempted to cross into southern Syria and establish outposts, including around Hader and Mount Hermon, with their stated ambitions extending across As Sweida, Dar'a, and Quneitra governorates. More than 40 settlers entered the outskirts of Hader in April, while approximately 70–100 attempted to cross through Mount Hermon in July, followed by further attempts in August. Armed Conflict Location & Event Data indicates an upward trend in incursion attempts since April 2026, peaking sharply in July with six recorded events. Although the Israel Defense Forces have so far prevented permanent settlement, repeated attempts could increase pressure on Israeli authorities to eventually formalise such activity.
If either pathway materialises, further Israeli control and presence in southern Syria are likely to restrict civilian movement and access to agricultural land through additional checkpoints, patrols, and military restrictions. An expanded Israeli presence could also prompt resistance from Syrian government forces, as well as communities or armed groups in Quneitra and western Dar'a, increasing the probability of clashes around Israeli positions. ([Ynet 20/08/2025](https://www.ynet.co.il/news/article/bktp9qfyxx), [Ynet 16/09/2025](https://www.ynet.co.il/news/article/hyhslcujxx), [Jewish Policy Center 01/10/2025](https://www.jewishpolicycenter.org/2025/10/01/focus-on-the-druze/), [AA 31/07/2025](https://www.aa.com.tr/en/middle-east/israeli-finance-minister-calls-for-humanitarian-corridor-to-syria-s-suwayda-for-druze-community/3646880), [Reuters 26/09/2025](https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/israel-syria-talks-hit-snag-over-humanitarian-corridor-sources-say-2025-09-26/), [AP 29/07/2026](https://apnews.com/article/israel-syria-netanyahu-jewish-settlers-bashan-461c4c4f686d5cf74f0617a7e70ffa29), [TOI 29/07/2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/fringe-settler-group-sneaking-into-syria-in-bid-to-claim-land-for-jewish-outpost/), [TOI 11/08/2026](https://www.timesofisrael.com/three-settlement-activists-illegally-enter-syria-overnight-are-detained-by-idf/), [L'Orient Today 14/07/2026](https://today.lorientlejour.com/article/1541299/who-are-the-bashan-pioneers-the-israeli-settlers-eyeing-southern-syria.html), [Arab News 06/07/2026](https://www.arabnews.com/node/2649854/amp), [SOHR 27/06/2026](https://www.syriahr.com/en/383771/), [Enab Baladi 25/08/2026](https://english.enabbaladi.net/archives/2026/08/jordan-talks-fail-to-halt-israeli-incursions-in-southern-syria/), [EUAA accessed 28/07/2026](https://dip-aws.euaa.europa.eu/syria-security-situation/2142-territorial-control-and-main-armed-actors), [ACLED accessed 30/08/2026](https://acleddata.com/conflict-data/data-export-tool), [FP 24/07/2025](https://foreignpolicy.com/2025/07/24/risks-israel-druze-policy-syria/))

R1074.rationale: The 28–29 August mutiny in Niamey exposed growing divisions within Niger's armed forces that are directly connected to the counterinsurgency front line. Officers and units involved were based in Ouallam and Tera in Tillabéri region and in Dosso region, while grievances included mounting casualties in fighting the Support Group for Islam and Muslims (JNIM) and Islamic State Sahel Province (ISSP), as well as perceived preferential treatment of the better-equipped Presidential Guard. Subsequent arrests of soldiers from special forces units in Tillabéri and changes in senior military leadership indicate that the mutiny is already affecting forces deployed in conflict-affected western regions. These divisions are emerging as non-state armed groups intensify pressure across western Niger. Violence remains concentrated in Tillabéri and northern Tahoua, while increasing attacks in Dosso indicate southward expansion. Additional deployments around Niamey, further arrests or command changes, and greater reliance on forces for regime protection could reduce military presence or operational capacity in conflict hotspots, creating additional space for armed groups. Over the next 3–6 months, JNIM and ISSP could exploit reduced or disrupted security force capacity to intensify attacks in existing hotspots in Tillabéri and northern Tahoua and expand their operating space further into Dosso. Increased violence and military operations would generate additional displacement, disrupt livelihoods and access to basic services, and further constrain humanitarian access. ([ACLED 01/09/2026](https://acleddata.com/expert-comment/nigers-capital-rocked-failed-mutiny-attempt-could-jihadist-groups-benefit?trk=article-ssr-frontend-pulse_little-text-block), [AP 12/09/2026](https://apnews.com/article/niger-new-military-chief-mutiny-12ecef2a363e00f825274ca712ef948b), [Reuters 29/08/2026](https://www.reuters.com/world/gunfire-blasts-heard-several-areas-niger-capital-niamey-witness-says-2026-08-29/), [UNHCR 28/08/2026](https://data.unhcr.org/en/documents/details/123893), [Critical Threats 25/06/2026](https://www.criticalthreats.org/analysis/jnim-alqaeda-issp-isis-niger), [Critical Threats 03/09/2026](https://www.criticalthreats.org/analysis/niger-coup-russia-algeria-sudan-rsf-chad-ethiopia-drc-m23-fardc#_edne8b267e3d17767bea25c63dd73e9048626), [FEWS NET accessed 30/06/2026](https://fews.net/west-africa/niger/food-security-outlook/june-2026))
